video_title: How Ukraine and Russia Fight in 2026 -  Battlefield Dynamics with Dmytro Putiata & Rob Lee
gist: A Ukrainian UAS officer (Dmytro Putiata) and FPRI's Rob Lee, interviewed by the Perun channel, describe a 2026 Ukrainian front line that is simultaneously porous and resilient: two-to-four-man infantry positions hidden in tree lines and basements act mainly as sensors, drones cause the overwhelming majority of casualties, and UGV-based logistics and casevac are what let near-encircled positions keep fighting through Russian infiltration. The core argument is against drone maximalism - artillery, cluster munitions and combined arms are what force the tactics that make drones so lethal - alongside concrete detail on artillery survivability (2S1 losses, towed-gun toughness, PzH2000/Krab sustainment), the Starlink/mesh/Rasvet communications fight, and a warning that Russian advance rates may accelerate in H2 2026 on manpower.

insights.claim: The Ukrainian front line in 2026 has no mappable continuous trace; infantry positions average two to four men and are placed only in tree lines, forests or building basements, with nothing left in the open.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Force-structure and wargaming assumptions built on continuous manned defensive lines are obsolete; concealment and dispersion, not fortification volume, are the buyable defensive commodity.
insights.quote: There isn't really a standard front line anymore. It's it's you know it's impossible to map.

insights.claim: Ukraine's 2024 program of doctrinally-built platoon-sized defensive positions became irrelevant almost immediately because they were too large to man, sited in open fields with no concealed approach, and destructible by enough fiber-optic FPVs.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A cautionary case that large-scale fortification spending can be wasted if it ignores drone observation - relevant to NATO border-fortification programs now being funded.
insights.quote: Ukrainian defense positions are all all of them are in either a tree line, a forest, or in the basement of building

insights.claim: Ukrainian infantry positions no longer have interlocking fields of fire, crew-served weapon layouts or their own observation - they outsource observation and nearly all strike missions to drones, functioning closer to sensor pickets than firing positions.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Western infantry doctrine, training and weapons mix (machine guns, crew-served fires) is being invalidated in the highest-intensity theatre; buy sensors and small UAS over more small-arms firepower.
insights.quote: The infantry positions do not have interlocking fields of fire.

insights.claim: A Ukrainian corps head surgeon reported that only 2-3% of the casualties he treats come from small-arms fire, with the majority caused by UAVs, artillery and glide bombs.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Hard casualty-attribution number for anyone modelling procurement priorities: small arms are near-irrelevant to attrition, drones/indirect fire dominate.
insights.quote: maybe 2 to 3% of his couches are from small arms fire

insights.claim: Ukraine fights with tiny static basement positions not by choice but because mobilisation has failed to deliver manpower, and the guest explicitly frames it as the only affordable option rather than a preferred doctrine.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Tactics being copied worldwide as 'the future of war' are partly an artefact of a specific manpower crisis - be careful extrapolating them to armies that can man a line.
insights.quote: no one is interesting uh having three four guys in a basement for 6 months

insights.claim: Small positions still fight conventional close battles at times: four men from the 93rd Brigade held a single large basement for roughly five months and killed six Russians in one small-arms assault at a few metres' range, because Russians needed the site as a staging checkpoint for further infiltration.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Infiltration is logistics-limited - assault troops cannot carry ammo and water 15-20km, so they must seize intermediate strongpoints, which is where defenders can still impose cost.

insights.claim: Mining has shifted from strategic belt minefields visible from space to small, discerning remote emplacements - the guest's unit mined a tree line roughly 300m in front of a three-man observation post rather than mining at the position itself, because mines adjacent to a position are simply destroyed by mortars and FPVs.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Demand signal shifts from mass minefield-laying systems toward small scatterable/drone-delivered mine payloads; also degrades the value of large-scale breaching equipment.
insights.quote: we literally mined approximately 300 m away from them

insights.claim: Russian dismounted assault size collapsed from platoon to squad to fire-team across 2024 and then into 2025-26 infiltration by groups of one to three men who walk past Ukrainian positions rather than attacking them.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Explains why territorial change is slow but continuous; also means loss-count metrics of Russian vehicles understate progress, since armour is no longer the vector of advance.

insights.claim: Russia's biggest 2025 innovation was organisational, not technical: elite units such as Rubicon built an echeloned drone-line system assigning different UAV teams to different depth bands, letting Russia close most of the UAS employment gap that Ukraine had opened in 2024.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: The decisive variable in drone warfare is employment structure and echelonment, not airframe specs - an argument for investing in C2 and unit design over hardware novelty.

insights.claim: Russia identified Ukraine's UAV teams and their logistics as the centre of gravity and ran an aggressive tactical interdiction campaign - Rubicon working 10-30km beyond the line and ordinary motorised rifle brigade UAS crews assigned the 0-5km band - specifically to stop resupply reaching forward positions.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Interdiction of last-mile logistics, not destruction of combat units, is the modern breakthrough mechanism - watch resupply capacity as the leading indicator of front-line collapse.

insights.claim: Ukraine defeated the psychological effect of infiltration once units realised that holding and resupplying forward positions is sufficient - infiltrators behind the line can then be cleared - which is why 2026 infiltration is yielding less ground per unit of commitment than in 2025.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: The counter to infiltration is sustainment plus nerve, not more infantry - a cheap adaptation that has measurably slowed Russian gains.
insights.quote: as long as you hold your forward positions, as long as you can resupply them, you can sustain that

insights.claim: Russia retains the decisive manpower advantage, recruiting more than 30,000 soldiers a month while Ukraine has fewer infantry on the line each successive year, and drones can compensate but not substitute.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: The single most load-bearing number in the war: any ceasefire or aid analysis that assumes Russian recruitment is failing is mispricing the trajectory.
insights.quote: managing to get more than 30,000 soldiers a month

insights.claim: Rob Lee explicitly warns that Russian rates of advance may increase in the second half of 2026 even though H1 2026 was slower than 2025.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable call from a well-sourced analyst - a near-term marker to test against territorial-change data over the next six months.
insights.quote: I'm concerned that the second half of 2026 we might see increase in the Russian rate of advance

insights.claim: Even non-fighting infantry retain value as a denial marker: knowing three men occupy a tree line tells the enemy that axis is not free to walk, which drones alone cannot achieve because drone coverage of the whole battlefield is impossible.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Sets a hard floor on how far infantry end-strength can be cut in any drone-heavy force design.

insights.claim: Ground robots have gone from a 2025 novelty to standard force structure - most Ukrainian brigades now field a UGV company inside the UAV battalion, some have UGV battalions, and the trend is toward UGV platoons organic to infantry battalions.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A concrete adoption curve for the unmanned ground vehicle market: from experiment to organic sub-unit in roughly 18 months, with battalion-level demand still ahead.
insights.quote: most Ukraine brigades have a UGV company in the UAV battalion

insights.claim: Ukrainian last-mile resupply runs as a relay: UGVs deliver to UAV and Mavic positions, then heavy bomber drones such as Vampire fly the final leg to infantry, because a UGV that reaches the front line is likely to be destroyed.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A reusable template for contested logistics: match vehicle attrition cost to the risk band, with a machine-to-machine handoff at the kill-zone boundary.

insights.claim: Drone units, not infantry, consume most logistics because they inflict most casualties - FPVs, batteries and ammunition dominate the resupply load while infantry that rarely fight need comparatively little.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Sustainment planning inverts: the consumable that must flow forward is drones and batteries, not rifle ammunition.

insights.claim: Electric UGVs move slower than 10km/h, so a casualty evacuation from a launch point 25-30km back routinely takes eight hours or more, which is why the golden-hour trauma model has effectively been abandoned in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee and Dmytro Putiata
insights.so_what: Explains the anomalous killed-to-wounded ratios in this war and creates a clear requirement gap - speed and endurance, not payload, is the binding constraint on medical UGVs.
insights.quote: to evacuate an infantryman is wounded can often take 8 hours or more

insights.claim: Ukraine's First Medical Battalion runs a dedicated evacuation UGV company using gas-powered vehicles able to hit roughly 80km/h on good roads and cut evacuation times to two or three hours, and Rob Lee expects a broad shift to gas-powered UGVs in 2026, citing the US-built Forterra Lancer modified Polaris ATV.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A named, near-term product-category shift - electric-first UGV vendors risk being designed out of the casevac and heavy-logistics segments by internal-combustion platforms.
insights.quote: they can do Kazvax in like 2 to 3 hours

insights.claim: Wounded soldiers in the forward red zone frequently have to crawl kilometres to a yellow zone before any vehicle, manned or unmanned, can risk collecting them, because any vehicle sent forward is destroyed along with the casualty aboard.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Grim confirmation of why Russian and Ukrainian KIA:WIA ratios look unlike other modern wars - geography and drone observation, not just weapon lethality.
insights.quote: no one is talking about this golden two hours

insights.claim: Both procurement camps are wrong: neither drones-replace-artillery nor artillery-without-drones works, and the Ukrainian officer who spent a year integrating both argues effectiveness only appears in combination.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the drone-maximalist pitch driving many defence-tech valuations; the durable winners are integrators of legacy fires with UAS, not pure-play drone vendors.
insights.quote: when I combined all of that it was uh pure art

insights.claim: Drone observation cuts the shells needed per target from roughly fifteen to nine or fewer, making UAS an ammunition-efficiency multiplier for conventional artillery rather than a replacement for it.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: A quantified ROI for drone-artillery integration - roughly 40% fewer rounds per kill, which reframes drone spending as a shell-stockpile saving.

insights.claim: Killing a dug-in Russian artillery piece requires artillery to suppress the crew and the infantry shooting at drones with small arms, while drones destroy shelters and then the barrel with shaped-charge warheads - neither arm can do it alone.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Concrete mechanism for why counter-battery still needs tubes: drones are shot down by small arms unless the position is first suppressed.

insights.claim: No Ukrainian source Rob Lee has spoken to, including UAV brigade commanders, believes artillery is no longer relevant - and artillery is what stops motorcycle and ATV assaults that FPVs struggle to engage, as in an Azov corps action using artillery and DPICM against roughly 40 ATVs and motorcycles plus 7-10 tanks and BMPs.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Direct rebuttal to the thesis that tube artillery budgets should be cut for drones; fast small vehicles are a specific target class drones handle poorly.
insights.quote: artillery and DPICM can disrupt those assaults very quickly

insights.claim: The frequently cited statistic that 80-90% of casualties are caused by drones is misleading, because Russia only adopted one-and-two-man infiltration in response to the lethality of ISR plus artillery - it is not economical to fire a Tornado salvo at two men, so the drone share reflects target selection rather than artillery's obsolescence.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A key analytic correction: casualty-attribution shares are endogenous to enemy tactics, so they cannot be read as a straightforward procurement signal.
insights.quote: they're sending one or two guys at a time

insights.claim: Ukrainian artillery now fires less not only for economy but because opening fire invites Russian counter-battery by tube artillery, guided bombs, fiber-optic FPVs and fixed-wing FPVs - so artillery brigades have grown their own interceptor, dart and fixed-wing FPV teams.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata and Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Artillery units are becoming self-protecting drone formations - a structural change that expands the addressable market for interceptor and fixed-wing FPV systems.
insights.quote: it's not economically relevant

insights.claim: The North Korean deployment to Kursk in December 2024 is a natural experiment showing artillery's suppressive value: with Russian ISR overhead for the first week Ukrainian artillery stayed silent and the North Koreans pushed forward using their manpower advantage, but once Ukrainian guns resumed firing, artillery became the leading cause of North Korean casualties and forced them down from platoon-company to squad-sized assaults.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: The clearest available evidence that suppressing enemy artillery, not drones, is what allows mass assaults to work - and that ISR persistence is the enabler.

insights.claim: Counter-UAS remains unsolved: drone crews hide in tree-line dugouts that survive fiber-optic FPV hits, and the practical answer is echeloned - artillery plus drones plus electronic warfare plus AI-cued remote weapon stations - because nobody can afford 20 FPVs and three bombers to kill one drone position.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Frames counter-drone as a layered cost-exchange problem, favouring cheap-per-shot effectors and cueing over exquisite interceptors.
insights.quote: the best thing is to kill the archer

themes.theme: Artillery survivability and the loss data

insights.claim: In the host's sample of visually confirmed Ukrainian artillery losses, Soviet-era 2S1 122mm self-propelled guns made up a strict majority of Ukrainian SPG losses - roughly four to five times their share of the force - while long-barrelled 52-calibre 155mm systems such as PZH2000 are under-represented.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Empirical link between gun range/protection and survivability - a direct argument for prioritising long-range 155mm over short-range legacy tubes in any rearmament plan.

insights.claim: Both armies have swapped artillery composition since 2022 - Ukraine from roughly 70% towed to mostly Western and Ukrainian SPGs, Russia from mostly SPG to a lot of towed D-20s and D-30s pulled from storage - which usefully isolates platform effects from operator effects in the loss data.
insights.speaker: host (Perun) with Dmytro Putiata
insights.so_what: A methodological handle for anyone modelling artillery attrition: the crossover gives four data cells rather than two, so platform survivability claims can be tested.

insights.claim: Range buys time rather than safety: an FPV takes roughly a minute per kilometre so a gun at 20km faces a 20-30 minute strike delay and can shoot-and-scoot, but Russian fiber-optic drones now reach 40km, BM-35/BM-37 types go further, and guided bombs plus fixed-wing FPVs are the bigger threat than copter FPVs.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee and Dmytro Putiata
insights.so_what: Standoff distance is a depreciating asset as drone range grows - artillery survivability planning must assume the whole operational depth is contested.
insights.quote: Russians right now are flying with uh 40 km range with the fiber optics

insights.claim: Range's real benefit is degrading enemy counter-battery radar accuracy - Russian counter-battery radars are described as accurate enough to localise a short-range gun to about 200 metres, after which a fixed-wing ISR drone finds it easily.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Explains the survivability premium of long-range guns through a specific mechanism, and highlights the radar-plus-drone targeting chain as the thing to break.

insights.claim: Ukraine lacks enough long-range propelling charges, forcing artillery to deploy closer to the front than is safe or to fire less often - an ammunition-component shortfall, not a gun shortfall, is constraining Ukrainian fires.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A specific, under-covered supply-chain bottleneck: charges and long-range ammunition, not tubes, are the binding constraint on Ukrainian artillery effectiveness.
insights.quote: they lack enough uh long range charges and so art often has to come too close to the front to engage

insights.claim: Dug-in Soviet towed guns are far harder to kill than SPGs - protected by underground emplacement, bunkers, nets, EW and machine-gun-armed observation posts - with one effective Russian 152mm piece taking dozens of fixed-wing FPVs, dozens of artillery shells, five crews from three units plus SBU, and roughly 40 days to two months to destroy.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Explains the large gap between Ukrainian claimed and visually confirmed Russian artillery losses, and warns that cheap dispersed towed guns can be more attrition-resistant than expensive SPGs.

insights.claim: A US-supplied shell landing about one metre behind a Russian D-30 failed to kill it - the crew resumed firing within two hours and fired more than usual - whereas the same near-miss against a Krab or Bohdana would likely have taken the system out through armour penetration by fragments.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive survivability finding: the armoured, complex SPG can be the softer target against fragmentation, which should inform mobility-versus-hardness trade-offs.
insights.quote: Those guys open fired in 2 hours

insights.claim: SPG complexity is a sustainment liability - Ukrainian Krabs were grounded because an American-sourced transmission part in the Polish system carried an 18-month lead time, whereas an M777 has far fewer failure points and keeps operating after damage.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Availability, not survivability, can be the limiting factor on high-end systems - a live warning for any force buying complex platforms without a spares and diversified-supply-chain plan.
insights.quote: we can get you a part in 18 months

insights.claim: Video evidence systematically overstates artillery kills: crews stopped storing ammunition in howitzers after 2023 Lancet strikes, so a Lancet hit often leaves a hole without a mission kill - Rob Lee saw a 2S5 with a shaped-charge hole that remained fully operable.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A discount factor to apply to OSINT loss counts for artillery and tanks specifically - hits without ammunition detonation are frequently recoverable.

insights.claim: Ukraine is producing roughly 40 Bohdana self-propelled guns per month, which Rob Lee assesses is more than enough to replace losses.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Ukraine has effectively solved the tube-artillery replacement problem domestically - Western artillery donations matter less than ammunition and charges.
insights.quote: Ukraine's produc like like 40 bodas a month now

themes.theme: Ammunition mix - guided and wide-area rounds

insights.claim: Excalibur and Vulcano guided rounds have become ineffective in this war while laser-guided rounds remain useful - Russian Krasnopol is described as accurate and a top complaint of Ukrainian units taking direct 152mm hits on their positions.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: GPS-guided artillery is a degraded product category in peer conflict; laser-guided rounds and the designation platforms to support them are the segment with proven demand.
insights.quote: We all know Excalibur became ineffective in this war

insights.claim: Cluster munitions are effective and increasingly valuable precisely because electronic warfare degrades precision: a DPICM round that misses by 50 metres still affects the target while a unitary round does not, though DPICM is poor against armour despite USMC doctrine teaching otherwise.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Argues nations that renounced cluster munitions have a real capability hole that jamming makes worse - relevant to the reported Ukrainian request for tens of thousands of Turkish 203mm cluster rounds.
insights.quote: one DPICM rounds can cover a much larger area than one AG round

insights.claim: A Russian 2S19 SPG survived a direct DPICM engagement, which the Ukrainian officer cites alongside Rob Lee's Marine Corps training as evidence that the doctrinal answer of calling DPICM on armour in the open is simply wrong.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata and Rob Lee
insights.so_what: Wide-area munitions are an anti-infantry and anti-light-vehicle tool; forces relying on them as a substitute for anti-tank capability have a doctrinal gap.
insights.quote: DPS is not great against armor actually

insights.claim: Ukraine's technological dependence is described as fully reliant on Starlink, which can be jammed, while Russia is building an independent mesh-network communications system it already has success with - a structural asymmetry the Ukrainian guest treats as a serious vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: Single-point-of-failure risk on a commercial constellation is now a named Ukrainian concern; watch for demand for jam-resistant mesh and alternative SATCOM.

insights.claim: The real cost to Russia of losing Starlink was not the capabilities held at that moment - usage was still embryonic on Molniya and BM-35/BM-70 mid-range strike drones from January - but the forgone ramp-up, forcing a detour to alternatives while Ukraine doubled down and scaled its own mid-range strike campaign.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Rejects both the 'apocalyptic' and 'PR stunt' readings of the Starlink cutoff; the measurable effect shows up as a six-month divergence in deep-strike scaling, not a step change in Russian capability.

insights.claim: Russian Starlink jamming is real but crude and localised - installations using eight dishes across eight satellite bands, with a Ukrainian source estimating roughly 20 square kilometres of coverage per unit - and the main Ukrainian answer has been to find and destroy the jammers rather than harden the link.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Large, immobile jammer arrays are themselves targetable, which caps the practical suppression footprint and favours strike over EW hardening as the counter.

insights.claim: Russia's Starlink analogue Rasvet already has a first handful of satellites in orbit providing intermittent connection of perhaps a couple of hours per day to specific users in Ukraine, and Ukraine is attacking the ground segment - satellite control stations and, most recently, a pair of Flamingo cruise missiles into a facility making critical rocket components.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: A live escalation vector: sovereign LEO comms is now treated as strategic enough to justify deep strikes on space-launch supply chains - a template other militaries will study.

insights.claim: Drone-borne mesh relay chains give Russia a workable Starlink substitute, but they degrade with distance and with lower flight altitudes because of line-of-sight limits, making them good enough for tactical use rather than a full replacement.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Sets the technical ceiling on non-satellite deep-strike control and explains why Russia continues to invest in Rasvet despite mesh success.

insights.claim: Drone swarming and autonomy remain far behind public perception - only two companies, one American and one Ukrainian, currently let a single operator launch several drones simultaneously against one or several targets, and the Ukrainian guest explicitly says it is not scaled.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Putiata (Ukrainian UAS officer)
insights.so_what: A direct reality check on autonomy narratives driving defence-tech investment; swarm capability is at the two-vendor demonstration stage, not deployment scale.

themes.theme: Defence-favoured battlefield and what breaks it

insights.claim: Net territorial change in 2026 has been even slower than 2025 and advances by either side are shallow, implying dismounted or short-range motorised assault is possible but maneuver into operational depth is not.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Baseline for any ceasefire or attrition model: neither side can currently convert tactical success into operational breakthrough, so the war remains a production-and-manpower contest.

insights.claim: Both participants agree offensive operations still require artillery - Rob Lee says he does not think you can breach defences without it - which places tube artillery at the centre of any future restoration of maneuver.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: If maneuver returns, it returns through massed fires plus drones, not drones alone - artillery and ammunition programmes are not a legacy line item.
insights.quote: I don't think you probably breach uh defenses without artillery

insights.claim: The kill-zone concept now governs all movement planning - minimise rotations, use vehicles as little as possible, and never move inside it if a machine can move instead - which is the organising principle behind the UGV and drone-logistics buildout.
insights.speaker: Rob Lee
insights.so_what: A transferable planning primitive for any drone-saturated theatre: substitute machines for human movement inside the observed band.

insights.claim: The host frames 2026 Ukraine as a World War I analogue only in the structural sense - a cluster of technologies that initially favours the defender - and argues the open question for foreign militaries is how to restore offensive maneuver on a heavily surveilled battlefield without everyone dying, which is the subject of the follow-up episode.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Names the central R&D problem that will drive Western force-design spending for the next decade: counter-ISR and maneuver restoration, not more of the same drones.
